t.4.57.1: Thus addressed in piteous words by the monkeys who had given up hope of life, the vulture, with tears in his eyes, replied to the monkeys in a loud voice.
t.4.57.2: O monkeys, that Jaṭāyu, whom you have spoken of as slain in battle by the mightier Rāvaṇa, was my younger brother.
t.4.57.3: Because of my old age and because I am wingless, even though I hear of it, I endure it; for today I have no strength to avenge the enmity against my brother.
t.4.57.4: Long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had come to pass, he and I, both eager for victory, flew up through the sky to Āditya, the blazing sun garlanded with rays.
t.4.57.5: Spanning the path of the sky, we two flew on with tremendous speed; and when the sun had reached the middle of the heavens, Jaṭāyu began to sink down, exhausted.
t.4.57.6: Seeing that brother of mine tormented by the rays of the sun and utterly distraught, I covered him with my two wings out of affection.
t.4.57.7: O best of vānaras, with my wings burnt away I fell upon the Vindhya. Dwelling here, I have had no tidings of my brother.
t.4.57.8: Thus addressed then by Saṃpāti, the brother of Jaṭāyus, the crown prince Aṅgada, of great wisdom, replied to him.
t.4.57.9: If you are the brother of Jaṭāyus, you have heard what I have said; if you know it, tell me the dwelling place of that rākṣasa.
t.4.57.10: If you know of that short-sighted Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, whether he is near or far away, tell us.
t.4.57.11: Then the greatly radiant elder brother of Jaṭāyus spoke words worthy of himself, gladdening the monkeys greatly.
t.4.57.12: O monkeys, I am a vulture whose wings have been burnt away and whose strength is gone; yet by words alone I shall render Rāma the highest service.
t.4.57.14: This task of Rāma's is one that must be done by me first; yet my vigour has been taken away by old age, and my life-breaths have grown feeble.
t.4.57.13: I know the worlds of Varuṇa and also the worlds traversed by Viṣṇu's three strides, the clashes between the gods and the Asuras, and the churning of the amṛta.
t.4.57.15: I saw a young woman, endowed with beauty and adorned with every ornament, being carried off by the evil-souled Rāvaṇa.
t.4.57.16: The beautiful lady, crying out "Rāma, Rāma!" and "Lakṣmaṇa!", was flinging away her ornaments and shaking her limbs.
t.4.57.17: Her excellent silken garment shone upon the dark rākṣasa like the radiance of the sun on a mountain peak, or like lightning in a rain cloud.
t.4.57.18: Because Rāma's name was being proclaimed, I believe that woman was Sītā. Now hear from me as I tell you the dwelling place of that Rākṣasa.
t.4.57.19: A rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the very son of Viśravas and brother of Vaiśravaṇa, dwells in the city of Laṅkā.
t.4.57.20: From here, on an island of the ocean a full hundred yojanas away, there stands the lovely city of Laṅkā, built by Viśvakarman.
t.4.57.21: There in that city dwells Vaidehī, wretched and clad in silk, confined in Rāvaṇa's inner apartments and closely guarded by rākṣasīs.
t.4.57.22: There, in Laṅkā, guarded on all sides by the ocean, you will see Maithilī, the daughter of King Janaka.
t.4.57.23: Having reached the far end of the ocean, a full hundred yojanas, and having gained its southern shore, you will then see Rāvaṇa.
t.4.57.24: Make haste, O monkeys, and stride forth swiftly to that very place. Indeed, I see by my knowledge that, having seen her, you will return.
t.4.57.25: The first path belongs to the sparrows and the other birds that live on grain; the second belongs to the crows, who feed on offerings, and to those birds that eat the fruit of trees.
t.4.57.26: Bhāsa birds travel along the third path, as do cranes together with ospreys; hawks travel along the fourth, and vultures travel along the fifth.
t.4.57.27: The sixth path is that of the haṃsas, endowed with strength and valour and possessed of beauty and youth, and beyond it lies the highest course, that of Vainateya. And it is from Vainateya that all of us have our birth, O bulls among the monkeys.
t.4.57.28: A despicable deed has indeed been done by him, O eaters of flesh. Staying right here, I clearly see Rāvaṇa, and Jānakī as well.
t.4.57.29: We too possess a golden, divine power of sight; therefore, O vānaras, by the strength of our food and by our very nature, we can always see as far as a hundred yojanas and beyond.
t.4.57.31: Let some means be found for crossing the salty ocean; and having reached Vaidehī, you will return with your purpose accomplished.
t.4.57.30: By nature our sustenance has been ordained to come from afar, whereas the sustenance of those who fight with their feet has been ordained close at hand, at the very foot.
t.4.57.32: I wish to be led by you to the sea, the abode of Varuṇa. There I shall offer water to my great-souled brother who has gone to heaven.
t.4.57.34: Having brought the lord of birds back once more to that place, the monkeys, having obtained the news, became delighted.
t.4.57.33: Then the monkeys of exceedingly great vigor carried Sampāti, whose wings had been burnt away, to that spot on the shore of the ocean, lord of rivers and streams.
